title: Staging-to-Edge Tunnel Patterns and Minimal TF Adapter Notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft that captures a compact set of reference tunnel/topology patterns for moving tenants from staging environments into edge or customer-hosted VPCs with minimal operator friction. The intent is to:
- give solutions/SEs a small menu of supported patterns with tradeoffs
- provide a tiny TF adapter sketch that operators can drop into customer TF stacks
- include pragmatic cutover and rollback steps for upgrades

Context and assumptions (short):
- Customers may be airgapped, partially public, or have egress controls (common).
- We prefer not to ship heavy agents when a simple tunnel or reverse-proxy preserves data-in-customer-network constraints.
- Goal: reduce onboarding time to a 2–3 hour lab for predictable tenants; keep ops surface area low.
- This is targeted at Redwood Private deployments (VPC + on-prem connect) where infra teams own TF.

Patterns (high level) — pick one based on constraints:
1) Stranded GRE/VXLAN L2 Tunnel (low-L7 dependency)
  - Use case: tenant needs L2 adjacency for legacy appliances or flat multicast between staging and edge.
  - Pros: transparent to apps, minimal app changes.
  - Cons: often blocked by tenant security; monitoring is harder; MTU/troubleshooting pain.
  - When to avoid: if customer disallows layer-2 or transit provider disallows GRE.
  - Ops notes: test with small MTU first, ensure BFD/keepalives.

2) mTLS-tunneled API Gateway (recommended default)
  - Use case: modern microservices where HTTP(S) is acceptable and customer requires TLS+mutual auth.
  - Pattern: customer-hosted edge reverse-proxy (Envoy/Nginx) -> mTLS to Redwood ingress -> route to tenant runtime.
  - Pros: observability (tracing/metrics), easy to rate-limit, friendly with WAF/IDS, simple retry semantics.
  - Cons: requires TLS termination coordination and cert management.
  - Ops notes: use ACME with DNS-01 where feasible, otherwise short-lived cert rotation via KMS/HSM.

3) SSH-multiplexed SOCKS/Reverse Tunnel (falls back for strict egress)
  - Use case: customer only allows outbound SSH-like egress to fixed IPs; ephemeral tunnels preferred.
  - Pros: works in very restrictive networks, simple to script, minimal infra changes.
  - Cons: less scalable, harder to monitor, not ideal for high throughput.
  - Ops notes: pair with autoscaling worker pools on Redwood side; ensure session persistence and supervisor restarts.

Minimal operator TF adapter (design goals)
- One tiny module: accepts a single input block describing the chosen pattern and emits the minimal resources to satisfy Redwood's onboarding checks (ip allowlist, cert thumbprint, static egress IP).
- Keep the module <= 50 lines where possible; avoid embedding provider-specific heavy-lifts.
- Provide example snippets for each pattern — operators copy-paste and adapt.

Example: module interface sketch (semantic pseudo-tf, keep it small):

# module: redwood_edge_adapter

variable "pattern" { type = string }
variable "redwood_ingress_ips" { type = list(string) }
variable "cert_thumbprint" { type = string }

# minimal outputs: allowlist entry + optional reverse-proxy config blob
output "allowlist_entries" { value = local.allowlist }

# inside module (implementation notes in comments):
# - pattern == "mtls_gateway" -> create security group rules and upload cert metadata to customer vault
# - pattern == "ssh_tunnel" -> create an ephemeral compute instance with a small systemd unit to maintain reverse ssh
# - pattern == "vxlan" -> provision tunneled interface resource where cloud supports it (GCP/OCI)

# We intentionally do NOT manage the customer's reverse-proxy full config; instead we provide templated snippets and validation checks.

Minimal snippet for mTLS gateway (template to paste in customer repo):
resource "aws_security_group_rule" "allow_redwood_ingress" {
  type              = "ingress"
  from_port         = 443
  to_port           = 443
  protocol          = "tcp"
  cidr_blocks       = var.redwood_ingress_ips # operator replaces with module output
  description       = "allow Redwood mgmt ingress for tenant"
}

# cert handling note:
# - If customer has KMS/HSM: store Redwood public thumbprint and use their cert manager to provision mTLS certs to the reverse proxy.
# - If not: fall back to short-lived certs issued by Redwood with strict rotation (ex: 24h).

Operational cutover checklist (shortform):
- [ ] Confirm tenant account + model pins in Redwood Console (or API).
- [ ] Agree on pattern and record redwood_ingress_ips and CA thumbprint in TF variables.
- [ ] Deploy TF adapter in a staging tenant VPC, run smoke tests (auth + small inference call).
- [ ] Run load probe at target qps for 5m to ensure tail latency within SLO.
- [ ] Schedule DNS cutover windows (if gateway pattern).
- [ ] Finalize monitoring hooks (prometheus scrape points or pushgateway, logs to S3/ELK).
- [ ] Cut traffic, monitor 15m, rollback if 5xx rate > 1% or P95 latency regresses > 2x.

Rollback plan (practical):
- If traffic cut causes errors: flip traffic back to staging endpoint or toggle feature flag in Redwood Console that routes tenant to hosted fallback.
- If TF changes broke connectivity: apply previous TF state (terraform apply using last working statefile) and restart proxy.
- Communicate with customer: 2-hour incident window SLA for rollback ops in initial onboarding; escalate to SE team if not resolved.

Upgrade plan (patching/OS/kernel/network):
- Staging patches first: apply kernel/OS patch on a single staging instance, validate tunnel/mtu/packets, then roll.
- For on-customer reverse-proxy updates: ship config as a benched patch to one proxy node, verify tracing/metrics, then cascade.
- For TF module upgrades: provide a migration shim that maps old variables to new ones; avoid breaking renames.

Testing matrix (quick):
- Basic auth/handshake: pass/fail automation for mTLS and SSH tunnels.
- Bandwidth/latency: 3 bucket tests (10 rps, 100 rps, 1k rps) with 95/99 percentiles recorded.
- Failure injection: drop 1% packets, simulate cert expiry, reconnect.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Do we standardize on a single cert rotation mechanism, or provide 2 supported paths (customer KMS vs Redwood ephemeral)?
- Add small reference terraform module examples for GCP and OCI (not just AWS).
- Build a lightweight connectivity validator (CLI) to run from customer environment that verifies ports, certs, and simple inference call.
- Tie rollback triggers to Redwood Console alerting so ops can automate fallback.

Notes to self / meeting fragments:
- 2024-11-20: talked with Priya — customer X's IDS disallows GRE; drop that pattern from default.
- 2024-11-24: Samir volunteered to prototype ssh-multiplex supervisor and small systemd unit file that restarts on disconnect.
- Keep this doc short + pragmatic; longer whitepaper belongs in Confluence.

References and snippets:
- small systemd unit example (reverse-ssh):
[Unit]
Description=Redwood reverse SSH tunnel
After=network-online.target

[Service]
User=ubuntu
Restart=always
ExecStart=/usr/bin/ssh -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -N -R 2222:localhost:22 redwood@INGRESS_IP -i /etc/redwood/id_ed25519

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Final thought: ship the TF adapter as a "lint-first" module — it should validate inputs and print clear next-steps rather than attempt to own the customer's entire reverse-proxy config. This reduces blast radius during onboarding and keeps SE time per customer lower.

-- Maya
